'''Network-based diffusion analysis (NBDA)''' is a statistical tool to detect and quantify social transmission of information or a behaviour in social networks ([[Social network analysis|SNA]], etc.). NBDA assumes that [[social transmission]] of a behavior follows the social network of associations or interactions among individuals, since individuals who spend a lot of time together, or who interact more have more opportunity to learn from each other.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1995-01-01|title=On the relation between social dynamics and social learning |journal=Animal Behaviour|volume=50|issue=6|pages=1441–1453|doi=10.1016/0003-3472(95)80001-8|issn=0003-3472|last1=Coussi-Korbel|first1=Sabine|last2=Fragaszy|first2=Dorothy M|s2cid=53184734 }}</ref> Therefore, NBDA infers social transmission if the spread of a novel behavior follows the social network of a [[Population (biology)|population]]. NBDA thus allows the study of [[Social learning theory|social learning]] to be linked to [[Ethology|animal behavior]] research that uses social network analysis. NBDA was introduced by Franz & Nunn<ref name="FRANZ 2009">{{Cite journal|last1=FRANZ|first1=M.|last2=NUNN|first2=C. L.|date=2009 |title=Rapid evolution of social learning |journal=Journal of Evolutionary Biology|volume=22|issue=9|pages=1914–1922|doi=10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01804.x|pmid=19702889|issn=1010-061X|url=http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:4340688|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and further developed by Hoppitt, Boogert, & Laland.<ref name="Hoppitt 2010">{{Cite journal|last1=Hoppitt|first1=William|last2=Boogert|first2=Neeltje J.|last3=Laland|first3=Kevin N.|date=April 2010|title=Detecting social transmission in networks |journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology|volume=263|issue=4|pages=544–555|doi=10.1016/j.jtbi.2010.01.004|pmid=20064530|bibcode=2010JThBi.263..544H |issn=0022-5193|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00578723/document}}</ref> An R package for performing Bayesian NBDA, [https://github.com/michaelchimento/STbayes STbayes], was published by Chimento & Hoppitt in 2025.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chimento |first=Michael |last2=Hoppitt |first2=William |title=STbayes: An R package for creating, fitting and understanding Bayesian models of social transmission |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/2041-210x.70228 |journal=Methods in Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=n/a |issue=n/a |doi=10.1111/2041-210x.70228 |issn=2041-210X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Implementation ==
NBDA requires prior knowledge about the underlying [[social network]] of a population.<ref name="FRANZ 2009" /> In an observational study, the order (or timing) at which individuals in the population acquire a behaviour or information is recorded. NBDA then tests whether the spread of information or behaviour is explained by the previously determined network or not. Because more closely associated individuals are more likely to interact with each other, information is assumed to travel along social ties. If there is a good match between the diffusion of information and the underlying network social transmission is assumed. Otherwise, it is assumed that information was [[Learning|asocially]] acquired (e.g. trial and error, mistakes, etc.).

== Application ==
NBDA does not only serve as a tool for the detection of social learning, but also allows the estimation of the strength of the social transmission effect.<ref name="Hoppitt 2010" /> In addition, several individual-level variables can be included in the analysis, which have potential influence on an individual's learning rate (e.g. gender, rank or age), and can also be used to model the effect of, and statistically control for potential ecological and genetic influences. NBDA has been successfully used in a number of studies to identify and quantify the effects of social transmission on the spread of behaviors in both wild and captive animal populations such as [[starling]]s,<ref name="Hoppitt 2010" /> [[Common chimpanzee|chimpanzee]]s<ref name="Hobaiter 2014">{{Cite journal|last1=Hobaiter|first1=Catherine|last2=Poisot|first2=Timothée|last3=Zuberbühler|first3=Klaus|last4=Hoppitt|first4=William|last5=Gruber|first5=Thibaud|date=2014-09-30|title=Social Network Analysis Shows Direct Evidence for Social Transmission of Tool Use in Wild Chimpanzees|journal=PLOS Biology|volume=12|issue=9|article-number=e1001960|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1001960|issn=1545-7885|pmc=4181963|pmid=25268798 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or [[humpback whale]]s.<ref name="Allen 2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Allen|first1=Jenny|last2=Weinrich|first2=Mason|last3=Hoppitt|first3=Will|last4=Rendell|first4=Luke|date=2013-04-26|title=Network-Based Diffusion Analysis Reveals Cultural Transmission of Lobtail Feeding in Humpback Whales|journal=Science|volume=340|issue=6131|pages=485–488|doi=10.1126/science.1231976|issn=0036-8075|pmid=23620054|bibcode=2013Sci...340..485A|s2cid=206546227}}</ref>

== Examples ==
* Lobtail-feeding in humpback whales<ref name="Allen 2013" />
* Foraging strategies in tits<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Aplin|first1=Lucy M.|last2=Farine|first2=Damien R.|last3=Morand-Ferron|first3=Julie|last4=Cockburn|first4=Andrew|last5=Thornton|first5=Alex|last6=Sheldon|first6=Ben C.|date=2014-12-03|title=Experimentally induced innovations lead to persistent culture via conformity in wild birds|journal=Nature|volume=518|issue=7540|pages=538–541|doi=10.1038/nature13998|pmid=25470065|pmc=4344839|bibcode=2015Natur.518..538A |issn=0028-0836}}</ref>
* Moss-sponging in chimpanzees<ref name="Hobaiter 2014" />
